newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines Bradies exchanged.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines Bradies exchanged.

text.p: The Philippines was the focus in Asian debt markets Monday with the republic announcing the results of its Brady bond exchange offer.
The Bradies will be exchanged for 20-year uncollateralised fixed rate bonds but an offer for floating rate notes was cancelled due to insufficient demand.

The new bonds pay a semi-annual coupon of 8.75 percent and were priced at 95.481 to yield 9.25 percent. That represents a spread of 225 basis points over the 7.00 percent U.S. Treasury benchmark, the minimum return that was promised.
The 15-year FRN offer was suspended because there was not enough investor interest to boost the issue above the minimum US$200 million stipulated in the exchange offer.
Arranger J.P. Morgan said last week that investors that submitted bids for a cancelled issue would have the option to participate in the other issue at the applicable exchange value.

Bankers in Hong Kong speculated that the FRN failed to entice much demand because the pricing, while attractive if the Philippines redeemed the notes at the seven-year call, may not have been generous enough for 15 years.
The FRNs were to pay a minimum of 175 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate.
More likely, however, is that investors preferred the fixed-rate bonds because they are more easily traded in the secondary market than floating paper, a syndicate manager said.
The maximum aggregate amount of the fixed rate bonds to be issued is US$690 million.

Dealers said the 20-year bonds were priced tightly versus outstanding Philippine paper and compared with the issues of similarly rated sovereigns. But there were good reasons to take the new bonds, they said.

"Part of the reason why the deal was attractive was the feeling that if you kept the Bradies, you wouldn't be able to participate in the credit improvement in the Philippines," a Hong Kong banker explained.

Sources also pointed out that some banks holding onto the Brady paper are receiving a coupon lower than their funding costs, so the yield pick-up on the new bonds is attractive if not incredibly generous.
The Philippine par bond due December 2017 pays a coupon of 6.25 percent. The stripped yield on the par bond is close to the 225 basis points offered on the new bond, bankers noted.
Traders said the 20-year deal extends the yield curve for Philippine paper, but not everyone is sure the new bond creates a new benchmark for the country.

"It's an unusual maturity, and how much of a benchmark it will provide for other issues, I dont know," said a capital markets manager, adding "how many other issues of this maturity are there going to be?"
Other Philippine fixed-rate deals coming up include a Yankee for National Power Corp (Napocor) via Salomon Brothers and a Eurobond for corporate JG Summit through ING Barings.
The Napocor deal will be the first Philippine issue to be fully registered in the U.S. The sovereign deal is a 144a.
In other Asian debt news, South Korea's Daewoo Corp set a 200 million mark three-year bond.
